08:15 Local Time, 06:15 GMT, 11:45 IST: The coloured jerseys, the white balls and the slam-bang stuff can take a pause for the next three weeks as two of the world's best lock horns in cricket's OG format. The stakes are always high when these two clash, perhaps because there is so much similarity in the way they approach Test cricket - the fast, bouncy conditions they thrive in, the emphasis on pace and the fierce competitiveness that runs through both sides. The last time these two met in a Test, it was the WTC final at Lord's - and what a game that was. South Africa came from behind to stun Australia by five wickets and in the process claimed their first ICC title. Now, more than a year on, the two sides meet again, this time with a three-Test series on the line. Hello and welcome to the first Test between South Africa and Australia..

It has been a while since either side played Test cricket. South Africa's last series came against India in November 2025, while Australia drew a home series against Bangladesh a couple of months ago. And for Australia, this is their first Test tour of South Africa since 2018 - yes, that infamous series, the one forever etched in cricketing memory as Sandpaper Gate. A lot has changed since then, but the need to win especially in the opposition's backyard remains just as high. With the next WTC final set to be played at The Oval, both sides will know that every Test between now and then could prove crucial in the race to get back to the biggest stage.

South Africa have already announced their XI, with Anrich Nortje set to make his Test comeback after three and a half years. It was touch and go with Rabada, who has been working his way back from a hamstring injury and had only just started bowling in the last couple of days, but Bavuma and the team management decided against risking their premier quick. The more interesting call, though, is the inclusion of two spinners in Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer. Kingsmead can offer more assistance to spin than some of the other venues in South Africa, and that could well have played a part in the selection. It also adds an interesting dimension to a side that will otherwise rely heavily on its pace attack.

Temba Bavuma, as a leader, has been a revelation. He did something no previous South African captain could - get his hands on an ICC title. And since that triumph at Lord's, South Africa have continued to grow as a Test side, drawing a series in Pakistan and then whitewashing India 2-0 at home. One of the most admirable things about Bavuma has been his ability to get the best out of a relatively inexperienced batting line-up. The likes of Tristan Stubbs, Ryan Rickelton and David Bedingham have played fewer than 20 Tests each, but all three have put their hands up at various points. They will have to do it again in this series, particularly with South Africa's bowling attack slightly weakened by the absence of their spearhead Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi.

Unlike South Africa, Australia are yet to name their XI. There shouldn't be too many surprises in the bowling department, but the interesting bit will be who comes in for Green. Matt Renshaw made his comeback in the second Test against Bangladesh and despite failing in his only innings, could be given a longer rope. The practice game has offered a few clues too. Labuschagne's hundred and his position in the batting order suggest he could cling on to that No. 3 spot, while Cooper Connolly batted at seven and Webster at five. Will Australia stick with that combination, or will Nic Maddinson, back in the national set-up, get the nod for his experience? The toss isn't far away and we won't have to wait too long for those answers.
